description: A May 2017 paper in the Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers by Mike Black, Crossrail's Head of Geotechnics, on how geotechnical risk was handled in the central tunnelled section of the £14.8 billion Elizabeth line across London. Coverage: the tunnels and underground stations in the London basin, through Chalk, Thanet Sand, the Lambeth Group, and Harwich and London Clay formations. Methods: hazards were listed first (groundwater, hard layers, aggressive ground, old piles, wells and boreholes, abrasive ground and unexploded ordnance); ground investigations over many years drilled 1,906 exploratory holes, about 38 km of boring, 381 of them rotary cored, with 1,200 groundwater monitoring installations; 1,084 third-party logs were added to the geotechnical database; Arup led route-wide interpretative reporting and the British Geological Survey built a 3D ground model for Farringdon station. Outcome: hazards were mostly less severe than feared, groundwater mattered most, and issues were minor for the programme. Format and access: a free PDF on the Crossrail Learning Legacy site. Licence and cost: free to read; ICE Publishing reserves rights. Caveats: the geotechnical database itself is not published. Useful for resilience studies of underground transit, as a record of ground hazards and investigation density for a metro tunnel. It relates to the BGS geotechnical site investigation records in the catalogue.
